content: 1. HDV RNA levels in individuals with HDV infection can vary over time. This variability should be taken into account in clinical practice, and repeat testing may be necessary to confirm ongoing active infection or potential clearance of HDV RNA. 2. Monitoring and evaluation systems for HDV testing approaches, including universal and risk-based strategies, as well as laboratory-based reflex testing, are critical for improving the quality of care. Reports should be provided to healthcare providers and laboratory managers to enhance service delivery. 3. A database of individuals with HDV can be created using clinical or laboratory records and integrated into national HBV reporting systems. This would allow for better monitoring of testing, diagnosis, and treatment indicators. 4. High-quality data are essential to guide future HDV testing approaches and recommendations. Epidemiological studies on HDV should be conducted using quality-assured diagnostics and should represent diverse populations, clinical settings, and geographic areas. 5. There is a lack of data on HDV infection in children, adolescents, and pregnant women. Research in these populations is needed to address this gap. 6. Cost-effectiveness modeling and feasibility studies for universal HDV testing in lowand middle-income countries with varying epidemiological scenarios are necessary. This is particularly important in regions with high HBV prevalence but low HDV prevalence, or low prevalence of both HBV and HDV. 7. The diagnostic performance of HDV serological assays and nucleic acid tests (NATs) needs validation. This includes developing an international reference standard for key genotypes to evaluate assay performance across different populations and genotypes. 8. Priority should be given to developing anti-HDV rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) to facilitate decentralized testing and care, especially in lowand middle-income countries. 9. A target product profile for anti-HDV and HDV RNA assays should be developed to align clinical performance thresholds and operational characteristics with recommended standards. 10. Fully automated NATs should be developed to enable more accurate and reliable quantitative detection of HDV RNA across all genotypes. 11. The impact, cost-effectiveness, and feasibility of anti-HDV reflex testing on care uptake and linkage in different settings and countries with varying HBV and HDV prevalence should be evaluated. 12. The 2022 global health sector strategies aim to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health problem by 2030. However, as of 2019, only 10% of the estimated 296 million people with chronic HBV infection globally had been diagnosed, and only 2% were receiving treatment. 13. Addressing the significant gaps in testing and treatment coverage for HBV will require scaling up testing and case-finding efforts, simplifying and decentralizing service delivery, and promoting adherence to long-term antiviral therapy. 14. Historically, HBV and HCV testing and treatment have relied on specialist-led care in hospital settings. Decentralizing services to peripheral health facilities and community-based venues has been successful in improving uptake and reducing loss to follow-up, as seen in HIV care. 15. Simplified service delivery models for HCV, including decentralization, integration with existing services, and task-sharing with non-specialist healthcare workers, have been effective. These principles can be applied to HBV care to improve service delivery. 16. Strategies to promote testing uptake and strengthen linkage to care include using dried blood spots for testing, peer and lay health worker support, electronic reminders, and integrating testing into existing services. 17. Strategies to sustain adherence to long-term antiviral therapy include peer counseling, mobile text reminders, cognitive behavioral therapy, behavioral skills training, and medication adherence training. 18. Retention in care can be improved by using lay adherence counselors, peer and family support, and adherence clubs. These strategies have been adapted from HIV care guidelines. 19. Integrating hepatitis testing, care, and treatment with other services, such as HIV services and primary care, can increase the efficiency and reach of hepatitis services. 20. Decentralized testing and treatment services at primary health facilities or HIV/ART clinics can improve access to care. This is supported by task-sharing and differentiated care approaches. 21. Task-sharing involves training and mentoring healthcare workers and peer workers to deliver care. This approach has been successfully adapted from HIV and HCV care models. 22. Differentiated care strategies assess individual care needs and refer complex cases to specialists. This approach has been adapted from HCV care guidelines. 23. Community engagement and peer support are essential to promote access to services, address stigma and discrimination, and strengthen linkage to care. 24. Evidence from HIV care shows that decentralized and integrated care models improve testing and treatment uptake, adherence, and retention in care. These findings can inform HBV and HCV care strategies. 25. Peer counseling, text messaging, and cognitive behavioral therapy have been shown to improve adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART) in HIV care. Financial support can also reduce non-adherence and improve viral suppression. 26. Composite adherence measures, such as combining self-reported adherence with pharmacy refill data, provide higher sensitivity in identifying non-adherence. 27. Community-based interventions, adherence support clubs, and extra care for high-risk individuals have been effective in improving retention in HIV care. These strategies can be adapted for HBV and HCV care. 28. Tracing and re-engagement strategies, such as remote communication and in-person tracing, have been successful in re-engaging individuals who have disengaged from care.
